questions.question: When and where did Jakub Wojtczak die — the husband of Helena Bazelak and father of Irena (born 25 October 1932), Stefan (born 25 August 1935), and Kazimierz (born 10 June 1942) Wojtczak?
questions.rationale: The tree records a Death fact for Jakub Wojtczak but contains no date or place for it. His youngest child was born in 1942, giving a post-1942 lower bound. Polish civil registration death records, parish metrical books, and state archive holdings for the likely interwar/wartime period are the primary record sets; identifying the date and place of death is the direct and only objective of this project.

items.rationale: The 'Poland, Church Books, 1568-1990' collection (4135958) is name-searchable (personCount 30,945,552) and is the largest indexed Polish church record set on FamilySearch, covering Catholic and some Evangelical parish burial books nationwide. Searching for Jakub Wojtczak in death and burial records is the most direct first step: a matching entry would give the date of death and the parish, answering the question directly. The death must post-date 10 June 1942 (birth of youngest child Kazimierz). Coverage of burial records from the 1960s–1990s is uneven by parish per loc_001, so a negative result does not rule out a later death. Variant spellings of the surname (Wojtczak, Wojtczack) should be tested if the initial search is empty.

No location — parish, commune or town — is recorded for Jakub, Helena, or any of the three children in the project tree. Searching the same name-searchable 'Poland, Church Books, 1568-1990' collection (4135958) for the children's baptism entries (Irena b. 25 Oct 1932, Stefan b. 25 Aug 1935, Kazimierz b. 10 Jun 1942) will return the parish of baptism, establishing which commune the family lived in before 1942. That location then narrows all subsequent searches — particularly item 5 (civil death records) — to the correct USC office, state archive branch, and parish. The children's birth dates are known from the project tree, which aids matching.

Polish Catholic marriage records routinely state whether each parent is living or deceased at the time of the marriage, often with a death date or year in the margin or act. Any of Jakub's three children (Irena b. 1932, Stefan b. 1935, Kazimierz b. 1942) likely married in the 1950s–1980s. If Jakub had already died, his death date would appear in their marriage entry, making this a FAN item with direct evidence value for the death question. The same 'Poland, Church Books, 1568-1990' collection (4135958) is name-searchable. This is a required FAN item for a death question: the deliverable is what the children's records say about Jakub, not the children's own facts.

Geneteka is a volunteer-indexed database of Polish parish and civil records named in loc_001 as a key supplementary resource. It indexes many parishes and civil registers not yet in the FamilySearch corpus, including death and burial records. A search on surname 'Wojtczak' with given name 'Jakub' in Geneteka's death record index may return a burial indexed from a source not accessible on FamilySearch. This item is the fallback if item 1 (FamilySearch Church Books) returns nothing, since the two databases draw on overlapping but distinct source sets. Geneteka is free to search.

items.rationale: Per loc_001, civil death records less than 80 years old are restricted under Polish privacy law — as of 2026, deaths from 1946 onward require proof of family relationship. However, civil death records from 1942-1945 fall outside this window and may be accessible without restriction via Szukaj w Archiwach (https://www.nac.gov.pl/en/digital-archive/szukajwarchiwach-pl-search-the-archives/), which provides digitized state archive holdings. This item targets a possible wartime or immediate-postwar death. It is the fallback if Geneteka (item 4) also returns nothing, and requires the commune location to be identified first by item 2, since civil registers are organized at the gmina level per loc_001.

items.rationale: Earlier FamilySearch full-text searches located 1950-1951 New York passenger ship list entries for Stefan and Kazimierz Wojtczak arriving from Gdynia, Poland. Those images are browse-only (no name-indexed collection on FamilySearch covers New York Harbor passenger manifests for 1940-1960). The 'United States, Index to Alien Case Files, 1940-2003' (2540918, name-searchable) is the best indexed FamilySearch resource for this period: it covers USCIS A-files, which include alien registration records created when a foreign national arrived as a permanent resident. Searching for Jakub Wojtczak would reveal whether he immigrated to the US at all. Searching for Stefan and Kazimierz Wojtczak in the same collection may surface their A-files, which recorded a US sponsor or Polish next-of-kin contact — and whether Jakub was listed as living or deceased at the time they entered. A negative result for Jakub is itself evidence he did not immigrate, supporting a death-in-Poland hypothesis. The actual passenger manifests for Stefan and Kazimierz (already found via full-text) should also be browsed for the 'emergency contact' and 'nearest relative in country of origin' fields.

'United States, Census, 1950' (4464515, name-searchable) enumerates all US residents as of April 1, 1950. If Jakub Wojtczak was in the United States by that date, he would appear with his birthplace (Poland), relationship to head of household, and naturalization status. Helena Wojtczak's marital status in the census — listed as 'wife' or 'widow' — would establish whether Jakub was living as of April 1950. Stefan (born 1935) and Kazimierz (born 1942) arrived from Gdynia approximately 1950-1951; whether they appear depends on whether their ship docked before April 1. Irena (born 1932) may have emigrated separately; she should also be searched under 'Irena Wojtczak' and under any married surname. A Wojtczak or Bazelak household found in the 1950 census would anchor the family's US state of residence, focusing all subsequent searches — death certificates, probate, naturalization — on the correct jurisdiction.

'United States, Social Security Death Index' (1202535, name-searchable, 93 million entries) records the date and US state of last residence at death for all persons whose Social Security number was reported to the SSA at death. Searching for Jakub Wojtczak would directly answer whether he died in the United States and when. The three children all died in the United States — Irena (2011), Stefan (2012), Kazimierz (2022) — and their SSDI entries give the state of death, which focuses the next item (pli_010 NUMIDENT) on the correct state's death certificate repository and the correct SSA district for the SS-5 application. Helena Wojtczak should also be searched. A match for Jakub in the SSDI directly resolves the research question.

'United States, Social Security Numerical Identification Files (NUMIDENT), 1936-2007' (5000016, name-searchable) encodes the data from SS-5 Social Security card applications filed by each number holder. Pre-1973 SS-5 forms required the applicant's father's full name and mother's maiden name. If Stefan, Irena, or Kazimierz Wojtczak applied for a Social Security number in the 1950s or 1960s after arriving from Poland, their SS-5 application would name Jakub Wojtczak as father and may state whether he was living or deceased at the time of application, and give his country of birth. This is the highest-yield US source for learning Jakub's status from his children's own records. Search all three children by name (Stefan, Irena, Kazimierz Wojtczak) and search Jakub Wojtczak himself — if he held an SSN, his own NUMIDENT entry encodes his date and place of birth and his death date if reported. The state of death found in pli_009 (SSDI) identifies which SSA district holds the original SS-5 paper record for follow-up if the NUMIDENT image is unclear.

FamilySearch holds no comprehensive national naturalization collection for 1950-1980; the indexed state collections (Colorado, Maine, Massachusetts, Missouri, New Hampshire) are useful only once the family's US state is identified by pli_008 (census) or pli_009 (SSDI). 'United States, Index to Alien Case Files, 1940-2003' (2540918, name-searchable) is the best FamilySearch proxy: it indexes USCIS A-files, which include declarations of intention ('first papers') and naturalization petitions. Stefan Wojtczak (born 1935, arrived circa 1950-1951) would have been eligible to file a petition around 1956-1961 after the five-year residence requirement; Kazimierz (born 1942) around 1963-1968; Irena (born 1932) on a similar timeline. Naturalization petitions named the petitioner's parents and birthplace and stated whether each parent was living or deceased. If any child's petition lists Jakub Wojtczak as deceased, it establishes an approximate upper bound on his death year. This item should be executed after pli_008 and pli_009 identify the state, so any state-specific FamilySearch naturalization collection can also be searched.

Published obituaries for Stefan Wojtczak (died 2012), Irena Wojtczak (died 2011), and Kazimierz Wojtczak (died 2022) customarily name surviving and predeceased family members, often with place of burial or surviving spouse. 'United States, GenealogyBank Historical Newspaper Obituaries, 1815-2013' (2860782, name-searchable, 37 million entries) covers Stefan's and Irena's death years; 'United States, Obituary Records, 2014-2023' (5000145, name-searchable, 306 million persons) covers Kazimierz's 2022 death. An obituary stating 'preceded in death by his father Jakub Wojtczak of [place]' or 'survived by his mother Helena' would directly establish whether Jakub predeceased the child and possibly where he was buried. Any obituary naming Helena Wojtczak as surviving or listing a US city of residence would also anchor the family geographically, enabling the state death certificate search that a positive SSDI result (pli_009) would initiate. Irena Wojtczak may appear under a married surname — search under 'Irena' with a birth year of circa 1932 if 'Irena Wojtczak' returns nothing.

(1) straty.pl — Polish Government WWII Victims Database
URL: https://www.straty.pl
Search: given name 'Jakub', surname 'Wojtczak', date range 1939-1945.
This is a Polish state database of victims of the German occupation (1939-1945) — executions, camps, forced labour, mass graves. A positive result supplies date/place of death or killing, perpetrator unit, and victim category. Access is free.

(2) Arolsen Archives — ITS Nazi Persecution Records
URL: https://collections.arolsen-archives.org/en/search/?query=Jakub+Wojtczak
Search: full name 'Jakub Wojtczak'. Free public access. Covers International Tracing Service records: concentration camp registers, forced-labour cards, displaced-persons files, death notifications. A match establishes whether Jakub was a documented Nazi victim and may supply date/place of death and camp details.

(3) Grobonet — Polish Cemetery Portal
URL: https://grobonet.com
Search: surname 'Wojtczak', given name 'Jakub'. Free. Covers several hundred Polish municipal and parish cemeteries. A burial record supplies interment date (often equals death date) and cemetery name, which identifies the commune and parish for further civil/church record searches.

(4) Nekropolia — Polish Cemetery and Death Records Portal
URL: https://nekropolia.pl
Search: 'Jakub Wojtczak'. Free. Complementary to Grobonet with different cemetery coverage across Poland; also indexes some historical death notices.

# Locality Guide: Poland (1942–2000)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Poland restored as an independent state in 1918 after more than a century of partition among Russia, Prussia, and Austria; post-WWII borders redrawn in 1945 (eastern territories ceded to the Soviet Union, western territories gained from Germany)
- **Administrative center:** Warsaw (capital); death records are organized at the voivodeship (province) and gmina (commune) levels
- **Population during period:** approximately 25–28 million in 1942–1945 (reduced by WWII losses); approximately 38.6 million by 2000 (Gapminder/Populstat estimates)
- **Economy:** agricultural through the 1940s; state-socialist industrial economy 1945–1989; market economy transition from 1990
- **Ethnic composition:** overwhelmingly ethnic Polish Catholic following WWII population transfers; German, Ukrainian, Belarusian, and Jewish minorities significantly reduced or displaced by 1945
- **Religious denominations:** overwhelmingly Roman Catholic; significant Evangelical/Lutheran minority; smaller Orthodox, Baptist, and Greek Catholic (Uniate) communities
- **Key historical events:** German occupation 1939–1945; Soviet-aligned People's Republic 1945–1989 (records nationalized under state control); Solidarity movement and democratic transition 1989

## Boundary changes
- **1939:** German and Soviet occupation divided Polish territory between the two powers
- **1945:** Post-WWII Potsdam settlement: eastern territories (Kresy — Lwów/Lviv, Wilno/Vilnius, Grodno and surrounding areas) ceded to Ukrainian SSR, Belarusian SSR, and Lithuanian SSR; western and northern territories (Silesia, Pomerania, southern East Prussia) transferred from Germany to Poland
- **Critical consequence for research:** If Jakub Wojtczak's family was from eastern Poland before 1939, pre-1945 church and civil records may now be held in Ukrainian, Belarusian, or Lithuanian archives, not Polish ones. Post-1945 records for survivors who resettled in modern Poland will be in Polish state archives and USC offices.
- **Internal changes:** Voivodeship (province) boundaries changed in 1975 (49 provinces) and again in 1999 (consolidated to 16 provinces). FamilySearch Catalog uses the 1967 voivodeship structure for record organization.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Level and start:** Civil registration has been continuous at the gmina (commune) level since 1918 for all of Poland. The civil registration office is the urząd stanu cywilnego (USC). The FamilySearch Wiki has no dedicated Poland_Vital_Records page; partition-era start dates (1808 for Russian areas, 1874 for Prussian areas, 1918 for Austrian areas) are documented at [Poland Civil Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Poland_Civil_Registration).
- **What exists:** Death certificates (akty zgonu) have been issued at the commune level for all registered deaths since 1918, throughout the 1942–2000 period. The certificate records date, place, and cause of death; names of surviving family members; and personal details.
- **Privacy restriction:** Polish law restricts access to death records for 80 years from the date of death. As of 2026, deaths from 1946 onward are restricted; a family member must prove their relationship to obtain a certificate. Deaths from 1942–1945 are now past the 80-year mark and may be more accessible. ([Poland Civil Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Poland_Civil_Registration))
- **Where held:** Records within the last 100 years remain at the local USC office; older records are transferred to state archives once every record in a volume is past its restriction period. ([Poland Civil Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Poland_Civil_Registration))
- **Digitization:** No FamilySearch indexed collection covers post-1918 civil death records from USC offices. The digitized volume search for Poland 1942–2000 returned 2,452 matching volumes across death and vital record types; every volume examined on the first page is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Online order:** The Polish government portal at https://www.gov.pl/web/gov/uzyskaj-odpis-aktu-stanu-cywilnego-urodzenia-malzenstwa-zgonu allows formal certificate requests; addresses of all USC offices are at https://archiwum.mswia.gov.pl/pl/form/148,Adresy-USC-w-Polsce-Addresses-of-Civil-Registry-Offices.html

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (predominant); Evangelical/Lutheran; Orthodox; Baptist; Greek Catholic (Uniate) in southeastern areas
- **Record types:** Burial registers (księgi pogrzebów) recording date of death, date of burial, name of deceased, age, and surviving family members; confirmation records can establish family relationships and ages
- **Where held:** Records are at the parish level; older registers (generally pre-1900 or pre-1945) have been transferred to diocesan archives or state archives. The PRADZIAD database at http://baza.archiwa.gov.pl/sezam/pradziad.php?l=en shows which archive holds specific registers.
- **FamilySearch collections overlapping 1942–2000 (6 of 7 returned; one collection title unavailable):**
  - **Poland, Church Books, 1568–1990** (collection 4135958): 5.28 million records, 30.9 million persons indexed, 1.15 million images — **indexed + images; the primary online starting point**
  - **Poland, Lublin, Roman Catholic Church Books, 1784–1964** (collection 1867931): 310,044 records, 1.31 million persons, 397,530 images — indexed + images; Lublin region pre-1965
  - **Poland, Radom, Roman Catholic Church Books, 1587–1966** (collection 1407440): 101,352 records, 310,221 persons, 1.26 million images — indexed + images; Radom region pre-1967
  - **Poland, Evangelical Church Books, 1700–2005** (collection 2564996): 168,622 images, 0 indexed records — **browse-only**
  - **Poland, Częstochowa Roman Catholic Church Books, 1226–1950** (collection 2115410): 1.9 million images, 0 indexed — **browse-only**
  - **Poland, Gliwice, Roman Catholic Church Books, 1599–1976** (collection 2114433): 185,526 images, 0 indexed — **browse-only**
- **Language:** Post-1918 records are in Polish. Older registers from formerly Prussian areas may be in German; formerly Russian-partition areas may have Latin or Russian records from before 1918.
- **For death after ~1965–1990:** Church burial records for the later part of the target window are generally not in any FamilySearch online collection. Contact the parish directly or the relevant diocesan archive.

### Census records
- **Post-WWII censuses:** Polish national censuses were conducted in 1946, 1950, 1960, 1970, 1978, and 1988; these are population counts and are not accessible as individual genealogical records in any online database for this period.
- **Substitute sources:** Tax registers, church membership lists, and city directories can substitute for census years where census access is unavailable.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, intestate administrations, guardianship records
- **Where held:** State archives (Archiwa Państwowe); partially searchable through Szukaj w Archiwach (https://www.szukajwarchiwach.gov.pl)
- **Coverage for 1942–2000:** Limited online availability; primarily physical access at state archives

### Land records
- **Post-1945:** Under communist land reform most private land was nationalized; land records from this period are in state archives and local land registry offices, generally not digitized
- **Pre-1945 land records:** Held in state archives and partially accessible through Szukaj w Archiwach

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** World War II (1939–1945); Cold War military service (1945–1989)
- **Record types:** Military service records, conscription registers, POW records, war casualty lists
- **Where held:** Central Military Archive (Centralne Archiwum Wojskowe, Warsaw); partially online
- **Online access:** Poland Military Personnel at MyHeritage (https://www.myheritage.com/research/collection-20734/poland-military-personnel) — index + images, subscription required

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:**
  - Poland Gravestones at Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/62954/) — 1509–2023; subscription
  - Poland Gravestones at MyHeritage (https://www.myheritage.com/research/collection-10963/poland-gravestones-1800-2020) — 1800–2020; subscription
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at parishes, municipal cemeteries, and in some cases state archives

### Newspaper records
- **Online coverage:** Poland Newspapers at MyHeritage (https://www.myheritage.com/research/collection-11037/poland-newspapers-from-oldnewscom) — subscription
- **Content value:** Obituaries (nekrologi) and death notices appeared in local papers; physical newspaper collections are at the National Library (Biblioteka Narodowa) in Warsaw

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Record types:** Declarations of intention, naturalization records, alien registration documents — these were generated inland, not only at ports of entry
- **Where held:** State courts and civil archives; generally not digitized for 1942–2000
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record all family members traveling together, including infants. If any family member emigrated, search the full manifest for the complete family unit at NARA and Ancestry.

### Tax records
- **Post-1945:** Tax records under the communist system; in state archives; not accessible online
- **Substitute value:** Can help establish residence and place of living in years without accessible census data

### Other record types
- **Political victims database:** Poland Political Victims Search at https://indeksrepresjonowanych.pl/int/wyszukiwanie/94,Wyszukiwanie.html — for those affected by Nazi and Soviet repressions; free index
- **Chronicles of Terror:** https://www.chroniclesofterror.pl/dlibra — testimonies of Polish survivors of totalitarian crimes
- **UNRRA displaced persons records (1943–1947):** https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/61742/ — subscription; covers Polish displaced persons post-WWII
- **Register of the Władysław Anders Collection:** https://www.szukajwarchiwach.pl/800/1/0/str/1/15?ps=True#tabJednostki — testimonies of Polish survivors of the Soviet Gulag

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Poland, Church Books 1568–1990 (30.9M persons indexed); Poland, Lublin RC Church Books 1784–1964; Poland, Radom RC Church Books 1587–1966; Poland, Evangelical Church Books 1700–2005 (browse-only); Poland, Częstochowa RC Church Books 1226–1950 (browse-only); Poland, Gliwice RC Church Books 1599–1976 (browse-only) | Free |
| Szukaj w Archiwach (szukajwarchiwach.gov.pl) | Polish National Archives: civil registration and church records; links directly to scans | Free |
| Geneteka (geneteka.genealodzy.pl) | Volunteer-indexed birth, marriage, and death records from across Poland; index + images | Free |
| PRADZIAD (baza.archiwa.gov.pl/sezam/pradziad.php) | Finding aid: shows which state archive holds specific civil registration and parish registers | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | Poland, Roman Catholic Church Books Index 1742–1964 (index only); Poland Gravestones 1509–2023 | Subscription |
| MyHeritage (myheritage.com) | Poland Gravestones 1800–2020; Poland Military Personnel; Poland Newspapers | Subscription |
| Polish Government Portal (gov.pl) | Formal certificate requests from USC offices for births, marriages, and deaths | Free (ID required) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The digitized volume search returned 2,452 volumes matching death, vital, and religious death record types for Poland 1942–2000. The first page of results (approximately 100 volumes) was reviewed; a volume-type summary could not be computed due to a server timeout. Every volume examined on the first page is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). The remaining volumes were not examined.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Local USC offices (urząd stanu cywilnego) | Death certificates 1918 to present at the commune level; deaths within 80 years require proof of relationship | Write or visit; directory at archiwum.mswia.gov.pl |
| Polish State Archives (Archiwa Państwowe) | Civil and church records once their volumes are past restriction periods; some more recent records transferred earlier | In-person or via Szukaj w Archiwach; PRADZIAD identifies the correct branch |
| Diocesan archives (archiwa diecezjalne) | Parish registers not transferred to state archives; burial records for many parishes | Contact individual diocesan archive |
| National Library (Biblioteka Narodowa, Warsaw) | Newspaper collections including death notices and obituaries | In-person; some digitized at Polona.pl |
| Central Military Archive (Centralne Archiwum Wojskowe, Warsaw) | Military service and conscription records | Written request; some records being digitized |
| State Archives in Kraków (archiwum.krakow.pl) | Records for the Lesser Poland region | In-person or written request |

## Records NOT online
- **Civil death certificates 1942–2000:** Held at local USC offices or state archives; not available in any indexed online database. Deaths from 1946 onward require proof of family relationship to access.
- **Post-1965 parish burial records:** Burial registers from most parishes after approximately 1965–1990 are not in any FamilySearch collection; still at the parish or diocesan archive.
- **Polish census records (1946–1988):** Not accessible for individual genealogical research through any online database.
- **Communist-era state administrative records:** Employment records, residence registration (meldunki), and internal passports; in state archives and generally not digitized.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey specifically reports the destruction of civil or church death records as a class for the 1942–2000 period in modern Poland. WWII caused significant record losses in areas destroyed during the German occupation and the 1939 campaign; the fate of any specific town's registers must be verified through PRADZIAD and Szukaj w Archiwach. An empty search result in those tools means the record is not yet digitized or indexed — not necessarily that it was destroyed.

## Research tips
- **Know the town first.** Civil and church death records in Poland are organized at the gmina (commune) level. Without the specific town or village where Jakub Wojtczak died, you cannot identify the correct USC office or parish. Use Mapa.Szukacz.pl to find the commune, then use PRADZIAD to find the relevant archive. ([Poland Research Tips and Strategies](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Poland_Research_Tips_and_Strategies))
- **Use PRADZIAD as your first finding aid.** The PRADZIAD database at baza.archiwa.gov.pl/sezam/pradziad.php?l=en maps which state archive holds which civil and parish registers — it is the essential tool before writing to any archive. ([Poland Civil Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Poland_Civil_Registration))
- **Privacy law at the USC.** Deaths from 1946 onward require proof of family relationship to obtain a certificate. Order through the Polish government portal at gov.pl or contact the local USC directly. For deaths from 1942–1945 (now more than 80 years ago), restrictions have formally lapsed. ([Poland Getting Started](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Poland_Getting_Started))
- **Start with FamilySearch Poland, Church Books.** Collection 4135958 (familysearch.org/search/collection/4135958) is the largest indexed online source for Polish deaths, covering baptisms, marriages, and burials through approximately 1990. Search it before writing to archives. ([Poland Online Genealogy Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Poland_Online_Genealogy_Records))
- **Check Geneteka and Szukaj w Archiwach.** Geneteka (geneteka.genealodzy.pl) provides volunteer-indexed records with images for many voivodeships; Szukaj w Archiwach (szukajwarchiwach.gov.pl) links directly to scanned civil and church registers held in state archives — both are free and supplement FamilySearch. ([Poland Getting Started](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Poland_Getting_Started))
- **Consider the eastern border shift.** If the family's hometown was in eastern Poland before 1945 — any area now in Ukraine, Belarus, or Lithuania — their pre-1945 records are in foreign archives. Post-1945 records for survivors who resettled in modern Poland are in Polish USC offices and state archives. ([Poland Research Tips and Strategies](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Poland_Research_Tips_and_Strategies))
